notes: Independent local mathematical Audit A: the displayed derivation proves every N002 clause from H001, H003 and the supplied E statements, with the routine completions recorded below. All five checks and all 23 external applications were assessed. This is a conditional mathematical judgment; global source identity and execution attestation are separate.

applicability.notes: All 23 E applications have valid real-space bindings and available premises. The induction uses E004's forward implication, not its converse. E007 gives the stated direction order, E006 has C² regularity on open Ω, and E010 uses genuine open neighborhoods. E003/E012 apply to real sections and norms; BG006 justifies the vector-valued conclusion.

argument.notes: S001–S003 prove all required smoothness and the mixed derivative identity. H003 is applied to 0<t0/2<3t0/2; the single resulting C0 supports all orders and all times in the open slab. The S006 induction differentiates equality on an open neighborhood, avoiding boundary assertions. S007 identifies ordinary partials and proves compact support; S008 proves integrability, including vector/tensor fields. No time differentiation under an integral or other limiting exchange is invoked.

dependency_closure.notes: The only substantive premises are the listed H001, H003 and E statements. F001–F008 are established in order. The derivative-order inductions have a smoothness base and a zero-derivative base, respectively, and their steps hold for every fixed direction. C0 is chosen only after F004 and stays within t0's positive-time scope. S009 existentially hides C0 and discharges L1 before universal quantification. Smoothness and the mixed identity are derived without dependence on that witness. BG001–BG006 record routine completions without new H or a changed route; there is no circular or future input.

background_notes.fact: Ω=X×(0,∞) is open in Z. A total representative agreeing there with the given smooth u is C∞ on Ω. On an open set, C∞ regularity implies ordinary pointwise differentiability, continuity, and C² regularity.

background_notes.justification: The time projection is continuous, so its inverse image of the open positive interval is open. Every positive-time point has a neighborhood within this domain, where Uext and u have identical representatives. Smoothness is local and depends only on these restrictions. The definition of C∞ provides each finite regularity order; differentiability at an interior point is the ordinary Fréchet notion and implies continuity.

background_notes.justification: For a constant field, subtracting its value and the proposed zero linear differential leaves the zero remainder. Its derivative map is itself identically zero. Induction gives every derivative order and their continuity, proving C∞ regularity. This applies also to the constant q and zero fields used subsequently.

background_notes.fact: The chosen compact C0⊂X is closed and Borel, hence Lebesgue measurable. O0=(X∖C0)×(t0/2,3t0/2) is open and lies in Ω.

background_notes.justification: A compact subset of a Hausdorff space is closed: separate an exterior point from each compact-set point and extract a finite subcover to obtain a disjoint neighborhood. Closed sets are Borel, and Euclidean Lebesgue measure includes the Borel sets. A product of the open complement with the open interval is open; its time coordinate is positive since t0>0.

background_notes.fact: For every finite order k, the derivative-tensor codomain of maps Z→V is finite-dimensional. A k-linear tensor is determined by its values on tuples of a finite basis of Z. Consequently vanishing of every ordered constant-direction derivative implies vanishing of the full k-th derivative tensor on O0; its spatial sections have the same continuity as these finitely many coordinate fields.

All ordered constant-direction derivative fields are smooth on Ω by the E004/E005 induction.
The E010 induction proves their vanishing on the same open O0.

background_notes.justification: Expand each direction in a fixed finite basis and apply multilinearity: every tensor value is a finite sum of its basis-tuple values times coordinate products. Thus its finitely many V-valued basis entries determine it and identify its space with a finite-dimensional space of coordinate arrays. Fixed-direction evaluation is continuous linear; applying it to a differential remainder multiplies the remainder bound by at most its operator norm. Induction therefore identifies the tensor entries with the iterated constant-direction derivatives. Smoothness and continuity can be checked in finitely many coordinates, and zero entries force the tensor itself to be zero. This accounts for the derivative-tensor sections explicitly mentioned in S008.

background_notes.fact: If a field h:X→W vanishes outside closed compact C0, its topological support, the closure of {x:h(x)≠0}, is a compact subset of C0.

background_notes.justification: The nonzero locus is contained in C0, so its closure is contained in C0 because C0 is closed. This support is closed by definition and is therefore compact as a closed subset of the compact C0. The same argument applies when C0 is empty.

background_notes.fact: For a continuous spatial section h:X→W with W a finite-dimensional real normed space (including the derivative-tensor spaces), ‖h‖ is continuous and h is strongly Lebesgue measurable. If ∫_X ‖h‖ is finite, h is Bochner integrable.

The source is finite-dimensional Euclidean X with Lebesgue measure.
The vector target V is finite-dimensional; finite derivative-tensor spaces are finite-dimensional as detailed in BG004.

background_notes.justification: The reverse triangle inequality makes the norm continuous. Choose a basis of W; the finitely many coordinate functions of a continuous h are continuous, hence Borel and Lebesgue measurable. Truncating and quantizing these coordinates constructs finite-valued measurable simple maps converging pointwise to h, proving strong measurability. For a strongly measurable field, finiteness of the integral of its norm is the standard Bochner integrability criterion. Thus the scalar norm integrability proved in S008 supplies exactly the remaining condition, without any exchange of limits and integrals.

background_notes.fact: The affine maps x↦(x,r), s↦(x,s) and h↦(x+hε_j,r) are C∞. Their linear differentials are respectively h↦(h,0), h↦hτ and h↦hσ(j), so the latter two curves have ordinary derivatives τ and σ(j).

background_notes.justification: For a continuous affine map z↦Lz+b, subtracting L from its increment leaves an identically zero differential remainder. Its derivative is the constant map with value L; all derivatives of order at least two vanish. This proves smoothness and the stated differential and ordinary-curve formulas by direct substitution.
